title: Favourite restaurant or a new one?
allegory: A multi-armed bandit is like choosing where to eat every night in a new town: each restaurant's quality is unknown and meals vary by luck, so you must balance returning to your favourite against trying places that might be better.

chapters.name: Ten restaurants, one dinner
chapters.note: bonus section: nothing later depends on it

cap.1: New town, ten restaurants, one dinner a night. Go back to the best so far, or risk a new place that might be better? That's the whole problem.
cap.2: A multi-armed bandit: k arms, each paying out at an unknown average. Every pull spent testing one arm is a pull not spent on the best known one: exploration versus exploitation.
cap.3: A bandit is an MDP with a single state: no transitions, no credit assignment, just regret minimisation. It isolates exploration from everything else in RL.

cap.1: Keep one number per restaurant: its average so far. After each dinner, nudge it toward tonight's meal, by less and less the more often you've been.
cap.2: Reward averaging: track N (visits) and Q (mean reward) per arm. Q ← Q + (R − Q)/N is the running mean without storing every reward (Sutton & Barto section 2.4).
cap.3: Incremental sample mean: Q_{n+1} = Q_n + (R_n − Q_n)/n, the pattern estimate += step × error. A constant step instead weights recent rewards more, which suits arms that drift.

cap.1: A simple rule: most nights, go to your current favourite. One night in ten, pick anywhere at random, just to check you're not missing something.
cap.2: ε-greedy: with probability ε pick a random arm, otherwise the arm with the highest Q. Optimistic initialisation is another trick: start every Q too high so even a greedy agent tries everything.
cap.3: ε-greedy explores uniformly forever unless ε decays; optimistic init explores early and implicitly. Neither uses how uncertain each estimate is, which is what UCB adds.

cap.1: Smarter: give places you've barely tried the benefit of the doubt. Score each one as its average plus a bonus that shrinks the more you've visited.
cap.2: UCB picks the arm with the highest Q_a + c·√(ln t / N_a). Rarely-tried arms get a big bonus, so they get tested; as N_a grows the bonus fades, and ln t slowly re-opens old doubts.
cap.3: The bonus is an upper confidence bound on the arm's mean; UCB1 has logarithmic regret guarantees (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer, 2002). Guard N_a = 0 with a tiny epsilon, not a large one.

chapters.name: When feedback is late

right.title: Thompson sampling (random)
lines: draws a plausible mean per arm

chapters.verdict: With feedback an hour late, randomised exploration held up far better.

cap.1: Real life adds a twist: reviews arrive an hour late. Always picking the top score means picking the same place while the verdicts are still in the post.
cap.2: Chapelle and Li (NIPS 2011) tested on real Yahoo traffic. With a one-hour feedback delay, Thompson sampling accumulated 59,256 regret against UCB's 226,220: its randomness kept choices spread out.
cap.3: Textbook rule: UCB, with regret guarantees. Production evidence: posterior sampling is robust to delay, since a deterministic index repeats itself within the delay window. What you need: UCB, because tree search builds on it.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Bonus: nothing later depends on it
Explore vs exploit returns in DQN

cap.1: Honest note: this is a bonus. Nothing later needs it. But 'try new things or use what works' shows up again whenever an agent learns by acting.
cap.2: ε-greedy with a decay schedule returns in DQN; UCB's bonus returns as the selection rule in Monte Carlo tree search. Exploration also decides which behaviours an RL-trained model ever discovers.
cap.3: Regret minimisation is exploration in its purest form. It matters for steering AI because RL fine-tuning can only reinforce behaviours the policy actually samples: exploration bounds what training finds.

coda.title: Who gets tonight's visit under UCB?

params.label: c: how much benefit of the doubt

coda.f: [0.7 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/nA), 0.55 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/nB), 0.4 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/5)]

readouts.label: UCB visits tonight
readouts.f: (0.7 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/nA) >= max(0.55 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/nB), 0.4 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/5))) ? 'the favourite' : (0.55 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/nB) >= 0.4 + c*sqrt(log(nA + nB + 5)/5) ? 'the newcomer' : 'the dud')

caption.1: Set c to 0: pure greed, always the favourite. Raise c: the barely-tried newcomer gets the benefit of the doubt. Give it more visits: the doubt fades.
caption.2: Score = average + c·√(ln t / N). With few visits the bonus dominates; with many, the average does. Even the dud gets revisited now and then, because ln t keeps growing.
caption.3: UCB1's bonus is a confidence radius: it shrinks like 1/√N and grows like √(ln t), so every arm keeps being tried, but a suboptimal one only O(log t) times.

where_else: Monte Carlo tree search: a UCB-style bonus picks which move to explore next (PUCT adds a learned prior)
Hyperband-style hyperparameter search, which rations trials among configurations
Ad and news recommendation, where Chapelle and Li tested these rules on real traffic

hamming.what: A one-state decision problem: repeatedly pick among options with unknown average payoffs, balancing trying new ones against using the best so far.
hamming.when: When each choice gives noisy feedback and there is no state to navigate: ads, recommendations, experiment allocation.
hamming.why: It isolates exploration versus exploitation, and its UCB rule returns inside tree search; in this course it is a bonus you can safely skip.

object.title: The doubt ramp
object.subtitle: A ramp of benefit-of-the-doubt: tall where a place is barely tried, flat where it is well known.

cap.1: Across: how often you've visited a place. Deep: how many nights you've been in town. Height: the benefit of the doubt it gets.
cap.2: The UCB bonus c·√(ln t / N) over visits N and total pulls t.
cap.3: A confidence radius: proportional to N^(−1/2), growing as √(ln t).

cap.1: Along the visits edge the ramp falls fast: the first few visits settle most of the doubt.
cap.2: Doubling N divides the bonus by √2, so after a handful of pulls the average dominates the score.
cap.3: The 1/√N decay mirrors the standard error of a sample mean.

cap.1: Along the nights edge it barely rises: old doubts re-open slowly, so even a dud gets an occasional retry.
cap.2: The √(ln t) growth guarantees every arm is revisited eventually, but rarely.
cap.3: Logarithmic growth gives each suboptimal arm O(log t) pulls: logarithmic regret.

cap.1: Set the doubt to zero: the ramp goes flat. With no benefit of the doubt you're pure greed, stuck with the first place that seemed fine.
cap.2: c = 0 is greedy selection on Q: one unlucky first meal can lock a great restaurant out forever.
cap.3: Without an exploration term, greedy selection can settle on a suboptimal arm with positive probability.

cap.1: Double the doubt and the ramp steepens: you'll explore much more before settling down.
cap.2: A larger c trades short-term reward for more testing: it is the exploration dial.
cap.3: c scales the confidence radius; UCB1's classic form, x̄ + √(2 ln t / N), corresponds to c = √2 for rewards in [0, 1].

predict.q: Two restaurants both average 7/10. One has had 50 visits, the other 2. Which does UCB pick next?
predict.why: Same average, but the rarely-visited one has a much bigger bonus: more doubt, more reason to check.

predict.q: Your UCB agent throws divide-by-zero warnings on step one. Best fix?

options.t: Add a tiny epsilon like 1e-6 to N, so untried arms get a huge bonus
Add a large epsilon like 1.0, to be safe

predict.why: A large epsilon shrinks the bonus to almost nothing and UCB quietly collapses into greed.

predict.q: Feedback arrives an hour late. Which rule coped better in Chapelle and Li's test?

options.t: Thompson sampling: its randomness spreads the choices

predict.why: UCB re-picks the same arm until the delayed evidence lands; posterior sampling keeps its choices spread out.

object.where: Anywhere you ration tries under uncertainty: ad allocation, hyperparameter search, the selection step in tree search.
